rv.q: This is still a witty, vibrant, wonderful play, directed with layers of wisdom and an embraceable aversion to cartoon by Pam MacKinnon.
Twenty-six years after this play was written, Heidi's idealistic quest for fulfillment remains relevant, as does Wasserstein's incisive reminder of how hard it is to really change the world.
Those are, as it happens, key notes in Wasserstein’s durable play, and Ms. Moss and her collaborators in this sterling production sing them forth with a revitalizing warmth.
“I The Trees,” her Act I duet with Julio, is reason enough to put this very brief run on your to-do list this weekend.
That one monologue, to which Moss brings a real freshness and even some modernity, is Wasserstein at her very greatest.
And Moss’ opaque performance contributes to keep her at a distance.
But that isn’t what cheapens the play here — it’s MacKinnon’s production.
The play’s politics seem retrograde, but maybe there’s some comfort in that.
Now that we are 25 years away from the play's once-current finale, however, the pulse on which Wasserstein had her finger sounds fainter.

Even so, Heidi never really chooses or unchooses either, a frozenness that is at once Wasserstein’s central insight — transitional generations get chewed up in the machinery of change — and one of the play’s baffling limitations.
Here, Moss’ low-key approach verges on passivity, which doesn’t make the character especially interesting.

Now as then, “The Heidi Chronicles” is a sentimental exercise in punch-pulling that purports to take a tough-minded look at feminism and its discontents but never cuts close to the knuckle of genuine self-doubt.
The excellent company MacKinnon has assembled reminds us that Wasserstein's dialogue can be as funny as it is unsettling.
The subject matter is as relevant today as it was 25 years ago.
Even though this revival is clumsy about the past, its view of the future has aged well.
As Heidi navigates a rapidly changing culture, Moss is mesmerizing, natural and exceptionally expressive.

A new production of Wendy Wasserstein's Pulitzer and Tony winning play "The Heidi Chronicles" has just opened on Broadway with Elisabeth Moss of "Mad Men" fame in the title role. NY1’s Roma Torre this this review. In 1988 when it premiered, “The Heidi Chronicles” was revelatory.
Perhaps inevitably, the revival suffers by comparison.
It's hard to discern such nuances, however, when Moss' deliberate portrayal is blown off the stage by her co-stars' more vibrant work.
So why has Pam MacKinnon directed most of the supporting players around Moss as if they’re on a 1980’s sitcom?
The issues still resonate, but the first Broadway revival of this Pulitzer Prize-winner feels somehow diminished.
Its landmark status is intact, but its impact has been blunted by the years: Such topics are now everywhere on stage, film, TV and even in Patricia Arquette's Oscar acceptance speech.
It opened last night in revival at the Music Box, and, two and a half decades later, it’s still fantastic — searching, thought-provoking, very funny, and more than a little bit sad.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Wasserstein revival, praising Moss's performance and the play's still-relevant feminist themes, but many find the production dated and middling, lacking the urgency of its 1989 debut.

sg.ra: In a 1,023-seat house, rows E-L are the Goldilocks zone: close enough to read faces, far enough to take the whole set at once without the neck strain that rows A-B force under this unusually high stage.
A strong alternate to center orchestra — elevated, unobstructed, and closer than most mezz sections in a small house. Stay center; side seats face jutting boxes.

This is the small-house dividend: rows M-O still feel detailed at Music Box scale and cost less than the prime band. Skip row P if your show has a tall set, where the mezz overhang starts clipping the top.
A strong rake and a small footprint mean the back of the mezz still reads the stage cleanly here. Worth it if you'd rather spend the money on two shows than one.
The Music Box stage sits high, so these rows put you looking up for two hours and missing upstage blocking. Sources recommend them conditionally at best — skip unless proximity is the whole point.
